claims.text: High configurational entropy favors a single-phase solid solution in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid heating and cooling create kinetic constraints that govern formation and crystal-structure selection.
Differences in atomic diffusivity, melting point, and surface mobility cause insufficient atomic intermixing during rapid processing.
Rapidly processed, near-equimolar nanoparticles containing more than five noble-metal alloying elements typically exhibit phase separation and elemental segregation.
Segregation caused by insufficient intermixing produces irregular particle morphology.
Lower heating rates, intermediate-temperature holds, and slower cooling provide sufficient diffusion for homogenization.
The proposed intervention applies to near-equimolar noble-metal nanoparticle compositions in which no element dominates.
Entropy stabilization becomes effective once kinetic barriers to homogenization are overcome.
Local diffusion or mobility variations can create chemically heterogeneous regions and undesired second phases.
Atomic diffusion is kinetically limited under rapid heating and cooling.
Elements with different mobilities or melting temperatures fail to intermix uniformly and consequently segregate or phase-separate.
Slower thermal profiles permit atomic reordering that reinforces an entropy-stabilized homogeneous phase.
Slower heating and cooling will increase single-phase purity relative to rapid processing.
Slower heating and cooling will reduce elemental segregation relative to rapid processing.
Slower heating and cooling will produce more controlled particle morphology.
A more uniform structure may lower the thermal decomposition temperature.
The hypothesis is limited to near-equimolar systems containing at least five noble-metal alloying elements and processing timescales dominated by kinetic effects.
The hypothesis may not apply to alloys with a dominant major element or to bulk materials because bulk diffusion lengths differ from nanoparticle diffusion lengths.

contradictions.description: The initial state requires more than five elements, whereas the boundary includes systems with five or more elements, inconsistently treating exactly five-element alloys as both excluded and included.
